lesson.title: Genomics: Studying the Whole Genome at Once
lesson.summary: Genomics is the study of an organism's complete genome, all of its DNA, rather than one gene at a time, made possible by the rise of fast, affordable DNA sequencing.
lesson.body:
Classical genetics, of the kind Mendel practiced, typically studies one gene or one trait at a time, tracing how a single allele is inherited across generations. Genomics takes a much wider view, studying an organism's entire genome, its complete set of DNA, as an interconnected system. That shift in scale only became practical once DNA sequencing became fast and affordable enough to read not just a gene here and there, but millions or billions of bases at once.

Genomics asks questions that simply cannot be asked one gene at a time. How many genes does an organism actually have, and how are they arranged across its chromosomes? Which stretches of DNA are shared between related species, and which have diverged, a field called comparative genomics that helps reconstruct evolutionary relationships? Which genes are switched on or off in a particular tissue or at a particular stage of development? None of these questions make sense without a complete, or nearly complete, genome sequence to examine.

The Human Genome Project, an international effort completed in 2003, is the field's landmark example. It produced a reference sequence for the human genome and delivered some genuine surprises, including the discovery that humans have far fewer protein coding genes than many scientists had expected, roughly twenty thousand, only a small fraction of the genome's total length. The vast majority of human DNA does not code for protein at all, and understanding what that non coding DNA actually does remains an active area of research.

Genomics extends the tools of biotechnology from working on one gene to working on an organism's DNA as a whole, and it underlies applications from personalized medicine, matching treatments to a patient's own genetic makeup, to agriculture, identifying genes linked to crop yield or disease resistance, to evolutionary biology, comparing whole genomes across species to trace how they are related. Making full use of all that sequence data, however, requires computational tools built specifically for the job, which is the subject of bioinformatics.
